• #2

Mick — now that the deadlines have passed, I'd be interested in your retrospective on the bets and Ryan Robbins/UFO Jesus's six predictions.(i may have missed any public recapped you have made on)
The bet: In the 2019 podcast you and Ryan discuss an already-running five-year wager: roughly three years remained, and you said you had put the deadline in your Google Calendar. The podcast doesn't establish how the bet originally arose or attach a monetary value. Ryan later referred on Twitter to a "$50 bet with Mick West (that he initiated)", involving a head of state acknowledging "UFO reality," and said the precise terms were recorded on Twitter. I haven't established whether that was definitely the same bet or how it was ultimately settled. There was also a separate later $20 bet over the 180-day UAP report, which shouldn't be conflated with it.

Ryan's six 2019 predictions, due within six years:

  1. Disclosure would occur.
  2. Previously unknown UFO programs would emerge, older/other than AATIP and much better funded.
  3. More evidence would increase the odds that some UFOs are "not from here."
  4. UFO coverage would continue escalating into the mainstream rather than fizzle out.
  5. Many books would be written criticizing how skeptics/scientists approached UFOs.
  6. Disclosure would produce many scientific breakthroughs significantly helping humanity.

My provisional scores: 0, 0, 2, 5, 0, 0 / 10 — 7/60 overall.

Mick, could you clarify how the original five-year bet was formed, its exact terms/deadline, whether it was the $50 bet Ryan later mentioned, and what the eventual outcome was? And, six years later, how would you score Ryan's six predictions?

More evidence would increase the odds that some UFOs are "not from here."

We've had more videos and more verbal reports. We haven't had more "evidence". Indeed, it would be difficult to have less evidence, since the score so far has been zero. You talk about "increasing the odds", but the number of unsubstantiated claims is meaningless, since zero times a very large number is still zero.

Evidence does not work that way. Every time a purported 'UFO' stays unidentified it adds exactly zero to the probability of UFOs existing (or not existing): it's just 'no data'. While everytime a purported UFO evidence is shown to be mundane this decreases the probability the next 'UFO evidence' will actually be an UFO.

Think about this: every unidentified claim is a marble of unknown colour inside a big bag. Knowing there are many marbles inside the bag tells you nothing about their colour. But every time you extract a marble and you see it's black (not an UFO) this decreases the probability the next marble won't be black (an actual UFO).

It's maybe worth noting that "predictions" 4 and 5 describe something that the UFO community itself is doing: regarding 4, e.g. political actionism and PR treading in Elizondo's footsteps, and regarding 5, obviously what books they're writing is their choice.

Predictions 1, 2, 3 and 6 depend on actual facts, i.e. if there aren't any actual UFOs, they can't come true (and didn't).

The predictions (and possibly the interview, which I haven't watched) suggest a connection between disclosure and UFOs becoming more important to people. What we're observing instead is that we're not actually getting better evidence; just more of the "trust him, he's a trained observer" testimony and "3 fuzzy white dots aka "triangle formation" videos, plus the old (debunked) favorites on repeat.

So in a way, the predictions were wrong: UFOs don't have to be real for the UFO movement to gain more influence. It's a problem, and I don't see a solution.

Ryan's six 2019 predictions, due within six years:

  • More evidence would increase the odds that some UFOs are "not from here."

This is either a truism or is false. However, it's not a "prediction", as both sides of my criticism are from a purely logical perspective.

On one side, more terrible useless so-called "evidence" that's not actually evidence of anything adds nothing to support any claim of UFOs being things "not from here". You could accuse me of equivocation on "evidence" there, but it's not me that's doing the equivocation, that's the way Ryan's using the term. What he thinks is "evidence", I, and many others, don't think is "evidence". And more of that is as useless as all the prior load.

On the other side, actual good convinving evidence for a claim would indeed increase the credibility of an claim - but as I say that's not a prediciton, that's a logical truism, it cannot be false.

Just looking at it grammatically, that sentence tructure isn't even worded as an actual "prediction" - it's got a conditional embedded in it, for pity's sake. An actual prediction would be worded more like: ``there will be more evidence that increases the odds that some UFOs are "not from here".''

That's a fair criticism, particularly the distinction between "more evidence" in the loose sense often used in UFO discussions and evidence that genuinely increases the probability of the claim.

I think the attached report probably gives a bit more context for how I approached that prediction and why I provisionally gave it 2/10 rather than treating it as a successful prediction. My point there was essentially that the public record and official discussion expanded considerably after 2019, while the decisive evidence implied by "not from here" never appeared. But I can see the problem you're identifying: if "evidence" means genuinely probative evidence, then saying such evidence would increase the odds is close to a logical truism rather than much of a prediction. I was trying to act in good act viewing the claims as vague amd logically unsounded i may of felt they were in the most positive light possible.

I'm also new to posting here and fairly new to trying to write this kind of accessible/op-ed-style skeptical piece. The original report was attached to my first post, although I appreciate this isn't really a forum designed for dropping long-form articles into threads. If there's a usual convention here for sharing longer pieces, I'm happy to follow it.
After Mick's feedback I reworked the material into a five-A4-page magazine/article-style piece, mainly as an experiment in making the argument more accessible. I'm not a professional writer and don't have ambitions to publish it somewhere more formal; at most I'd probably share it here and in a few Discord communities I'm part of.

In any case, your point about #3 is useful. It may deserve a rethink in how I describe or score it.
